theme: World Literature: Epic Novels, Playwrights & Masterpieces
title: World Literature: Epic Novels, Playwrights & Masterpieces
description: A 60-question grand master assessment on ancient epics, Dante, Shakespearean tragedy, 19th-century European giants, gothic masterworks, modernism, American classics, magic realism, and Nobel laureates.

questions.question: What ancient Mesopotamian epic poem carved on clay cuneiform tablets is widely regarded as human history's earliest surviving literary masterpiece?
questions.explanation: The Epic of Gilgamesh recounts the king of Uruk's quest for immortality and his friendship with the wild man Enkidu.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek blind bard is credited with composing the monumental epic poems the Iliad and the Odyssey?
questions.explanation: Homer's dactylic hexameter epics chronicled the Trojan War and Odysseus's perilous ten-year journey home to Ithaca.

questions.question: Which Latin poet wrote the epic Aeneid to celebrate the mythical origins of Rome through the Trojan hero Aeneas?
questions.explanation: Commissioned during the reign of Augustus, Virgil's Aeneid bridged the Homeric legend of Troy with the founding of the Roman destiny.

questions.question: Which colossal Sanskrit epic, containing over 100,000 verses, includes the philosophical spiritual dialogue known as the Bhagavad Gita?
questions.explanation: The Mahabharata, traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa, is one of the longest epic poems ever composed in world literature.

questions.question: In Homer's Odyssey, what was the name of Odysseus's faithful wife who wove and unwove a burial shroud to stall prospective suitors?
questions.explanation: Penelope waited twenty years for Odysseus to return to Ithaca, demonstrating unmatched fidelity and cunning intelligence.

questions.question: How many traditional scrolls or books comprise Homer's epic poem the Iliad in classical Alexandrian editions?
questions.explanation: Scholars at the Library of Alexandria divided both the Iliad and the Odyssey into exactly 24 books, corresponding to the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet.

questions.question: Which Florentine poet journeyed through Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso guided by Virgil and Beatrice in The Divine Comedy?
questions.explanation: Dante composed The Divine Comedy in Italian vernacular using the intricate terza rima rhyme scheme between 1308 and 1320.

questions.question: Which 14th-century English author wrote The Canterbury Tales, chronicling pilgrims traveling to the shrine of Thomas Becket?
questions.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer is known as the Father of English Literature for writing in Middle English rather than courtly French or Latin.

questions.question: Which Spanish masterwork by Miguel de Cervantes depicts an idealistic nobleman tilting at windmills accompanied by his squire Sancho Panza?
questions.explanation: Published in two parts in 1605 and 1615, Don Quixote is widely recognized as the foundational text of the modern Western novel.

questions.question: Which Italian collection of 100 novellas by Giovanni Boccaccio depicts ten young people sheltering from the Black Death in Florence?
questions.explanation: The Decameron provided a vivid portrait of 14th-century life and profoundly influenced later storytellers including Chaucer and Shakespeare.

questions.question: Which 17th-century English poet wrote the epic blank-verse poem Paradise Lost to justify the ways of God to men?
questions.explanation: Milton dictated Paradise Lost while completely blind, portraying Lucifer's rebellion and the fall of Adam and Eve.

questions.question: How many total cantos make up Dante Alighieri's complete Divine Comedy across Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso?
questions.explanation: The Divine Comedy comprises 1 introductory canto plus 33 cantos each in Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso, totaling exactly 100 cantos.

questions.question: In which Shakespearean tragedy does the Prince of Denmark deliver the immortal soliloquy beginning To be, or not to be?
questions.explanation: Hamlet is Shakespeare's longest play, exploring themes of revenge, existential doubt, madness, and political corruption in Elsinore.

questions.question: Which Scottish tragedy by Shakespeare is traditionally referred to by superstitious actors as The Scottish Play inside theaters?
questions.explanation: The dark tragedy recounts the rise and bloody downfall of Lord Macbeth after hearing prophecies from three witches.

questions.question: What famous Elizabethan playhouse on the south bank of the River Thames in London staged many of Shakespeare's greatest masterpieces?
questions.explanation: Built in 1599 by Shakespeare's playing company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men, the Globe burned down in 1613 and was reconstructed in 1997.

questions.question: In Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, what are the names of the two feuding noble households in Verona?
questions.explanation: The tragic romance explores star-crossed lovers from the rival Montague and Capulet dynasties.

questions.question: Which Shakespearean tragedy depicts an aging British king who divides his realm among his three daughters based on flattery?
questions.explanation: King Lear is betrayed by his flattering elder daughters Goneril and Regan while banishing his genuinely devoted daughter Cordelia.

questions.question: How many sonnets did William Shakespeare publish in his famous 1609 collection printed by Thomas Thorpe?
questions.explanation: Shakespeare's 1609 quarto contained exactly 154 sonnets exploring themes of love, time, beauty, the Fair Youth, and the Dark Lady.

questions.question: Which French literary master wrote the epic social novel Les Miserables and the gothic romance The Hunchback of Notre-Dame?
questions.explanation: Hugo was a towering intellectual whose Les Miserables exposed poverty and injustice in 19th-century France through the redemption of Jean Valjean.

questions.question: Which Russian titan penned the monumental historical epic War and Peace and the tragic romance Anna Karenina?
questions.explanation: Count Leo Tolstoy depicted the 1812 Napoleonic invasion of Russia across sweeping aristocratic panoramas and philosophical essays.

questions.question: Which Russian psychological novelist wrote Crime and Punishment, exploring the moral torment of student Rodion Raskolnikov?
questions.explanation: Dostoevsky examined guilt, redemption, and nihilism after Raskolnikov murders a greedy pawnbroker in Saint Petersburg.

questions.question: Which Victorian novelist created enduring characters including Ebenezer Scrooge, Oliver Twist, Pip, and David Copperfield?
questions.explanation: Dickens utilized serial publication to expose the cruel social realities of Victorian industrial London while entertaining millions of readers.

questions.question: Which French realism pioneer wrote Madame Bovary in 1856, leading to a sensational obscenity trial before its widespread acclaim?
questions.explanation: Flaubert spent years obsessively seeking le mot juste (the exact right word) to depict Emma Bovary's tragic romantic disillusionment.

questions.question: In what year CE did Leo Tolstoy complete and publish the final serialized volume of War and Peace?
questions.explanation: War and Peace was published in its complete book form in 1869 after appearing in serial form in The Russian Messenger starting in 1865.

questions.question: Which 19-year-old English author created the science fiction and gothic masterpiece Frankenstein during the rainy summer of 1816?
questions.explanation: Mary Shelley conceived Frankenstein (The Modern Prometheus) during a ghost-story writing contest at Lake Geneva with Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley.

questions.question: Which Irish author published the epistolary gothic vampire novel Dracula in 1897, introducing Count Dracula and Professor Van Helsing?
questions.explanation: Stoker drew upon folklore and historical accounts of Vlad the Impaler to create the archetypal vampire of modern literature.

questions.question: Which American master of gothic horror and detective fiction penned The Raven, The Tell-Tale Heart, and The Fall of the House of Usher?
questions.explanation: Poe is recognized as the architect of the modern short story and the inventor of the detective fiction genre with The Murders in the Rue Morgue.

questions.question: Which English author, writing under the male pen name Currer Bell, published the landmark Victorian romance Jane Eyre in 1847?
questions.explanation: Jane Eyre challenged Victorian conventions through its fierce, independent heroine and her stormy relationship with Mr. Rochester.

questions.question: Which German polymath and literary giant wrote the two-part poetic drama Faust, depicting a scholar who trades his soul to Mephistopheles?
questions.explanation: Goethe worked on Faust across six decades, creating the supreme masterpiece of German literature and Romantic philosophy.

questions.question: In what year CE was Mary Shelley's landmark novel Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus first published anonymously in London?
questions.explanation: Frankenstein was first published anonymously on 1 January 1818 in a small print run of 500 copies by Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor & Jones.

questions.question: Which Irish author published the monumental modernist novel Ulysses in 1922, following Leopold Bloom across Dublin on 16 June 1904?
questions.explanation: Ulysses revolutionized stream-of-consciousness narrative technique, with 16 June now celebrated worldwide as Bloomsday.

questions.question: Which French author wrote the monumental seven-volume modernist novel In Search of Lost Time, sparked by the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea?
questions.explanation: Proust's In Search of Lost Time (A la recherche du temps perdu) spans over 4,200 pages exploring memory, time, art, and Parisian aristocracy.

questions.question: In Franz Kafka's 1915 novella The Metamorphosis, what does traveling salesman Gregor Samsa awaken to find himself transformed into?
questions.explanation: Kafka's surreal allegory opens: As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a monstrous insect.

questions.question: Which English modernist pioneer wrote Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse, pioneering feminist literary criticism in A Room of One's Own?
questions.explanation: Virginia Woolf was a central figure of the Bloomsbury Group who pioneered innovative interior monologues and temporal structures.

questions.question: Which American-born British poet published the landmark 1922 modernist poem The Waste Land, opening with April is the cruellest month?
questions.explanation: T.S. Eliot captured post-World War I spiritual disillusionment through fragmented polyglot allusions, earning the 1948 Nobel Prize in Literature.

questions.question: How many distinct volumes make up Marcel Proust's masterwork In Search of Lost Time?
questions.explanation: Proust's masterpiece consists of 7 volumes published between 1913 and 1927, certified as one of the longest novels in world history.

questions.question: Which American author captured the Jazz Age and the tragic illusion of the American Dream in his 1925 novel The Great Gatsby?
questions.explanation: The Great Gatsby portrays the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby and his obsessive pursuit of Daisy Buchanan across Long Island Sound.

questions.question: Which Nobel Prize-winning American author developed the iceberg theory of writing in works like The Old Man and the Sea and The Sun Also Rises?
questions.explanation: Hemingway's concise, understated prose stripped away extraneous adjectives, profoundly influencing 20th-century English writing style.

questions.question: Which Mississippi author created the fictional Yoknapatawpha County for Southern Gothic masterpieces like The Sound and the Fury and As I Lay Dying?
questions.explanation: Faulkner won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Literature for his intricate stream-of-consciousness explorations of Southern history and family decay.

questions.question: Which 1851 Herman Melville epic novel follows Captain Ahab's monomaniacal quest for revenge against a giant white sperm whale?
questions.explanation: Opening with the famous line Call me Ishmael, Moby-Dick combines whaling documentary, Shakespearean tragedy, and metaphysical symbolism.

questions.question: Which John Steinbeck masterpiece chronicled the harrowing Dust Bowl migration of the Joad family from Oklahoma to California during the Great Depression?
questions.explanation: The Grapes of Wrath won the Pulitzer Prize in 1940 and galvanized national attention toward the plight of migrant farm workers.

questions.question: In what year CE was F. Scott Fitzgerald's celebrated novel The Great Gatsby published by Charles Scribner's Sons?
questions.explanation: The Great Gatsby was published on 10 April 1925, initially meeting modest commercial sales before achieving status as a great American classic.

questions.question: Which Colombian Nobel laureate pioneered magic realism in his epic saga of the Buendia family in the mythical town of Macondo, One Hundred Years of Solitude?
questions.explanation: Garcia Marquez's 1967 masterpiece One Hundred Years of Solitude became a cornerstone of the Latin American literary boom.

questions.question: Which blind Argentine master wrote labyrinthine, metaphysical short stories collected in Ficciones and The Aleph?
questions.explanation: Borges explored philosophical paradoxes, infinity, libraries, and mirrors, exerting vast influence on postmodern literature.

questions.question: Which Nigerian author wrote the landmark 1958 post-colonial African novel Things Fall Apart, portraying Okonkwo in an Igbo village?
questions.explanation: Things Fall Apart countered colonial stereotypes and became the most widely read book in modern African literature.

questions.question: Which Japanese author blended surrealism and contemporary alienation in novels such as Norwegian Wood, Kafka on the Shore, and 1Q84?
questions.explanation: Murakami's evocative prose frequently incorporates jazz music, cats, parallel realities, and melancholic protagonists.

questions.question: Which Egyptian author became the first Arabic-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988, famous for The Cairo Trilogy?
questions.explanation: Mahfouz chronicled the social, political, and religious shifts of Egyptian life across generations in historic Cairo neighborhoods.

questions.question: In what year CE did Gabriel Garcia Marquez publish his landmark novel One Hundred Years of Solitude in Buenos Aires?
questions.explanation: Cien anos de soledad was published in May 1967 by Editorial Sudamericana, selling out its initial print run of 8,000 copies in days.

questions.question: Which English author wrote the chilling dystopian warning 1984, introducing Big Brother, Thoughtcrime, and Newspeak?
questions.explanation: George Orwell (Eric Arthur Blair) also wrote the political allegorical novella Animal Farm criticizing totalitarianism.

questions.question: Which 1932 dystopian novel by Aldous Huxley depicted a technologically engineered society conditioned by Soma and the World State?
questions.explanation: Huxley warned of a totalitarian state that controlled populations through engineered pleasure, mass consumerism, and biological caste systems.

questions.question: Which Ray Bradbury sci-fi classic depicts a future society where books are outlawed and firemen burn any that are found?
questions.explanation: Fahrenheit 451 follows Guy Montag, a book-burning fireman who rebels after discovering the transformative power of literature.

questions.question: Which Canadian author wrote the 1985 dystopian novel The Handmaid's Tale, set in the totalitarian theocracy of the Republic of Gilead?
questions.explanation: Atwood's speculative novel explores state subjugation of women's bodies, identity, and civil liberties in a fundamentalist regime.

questions.question: Which visionary sci-fi author wrote Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, which inspired Ridley Scott's film Blade Runner?
questions.explanation: Philip K. Dick's stories questioned the nature of reality, artificial intelligence, and human empathy in cyberpunk futures.

questions.question: At what temperature in degrees Fahrenheit does book paper auto-ignite according to the title of Ray Bradbury's classic novel?
questions.explanation: Bradbury chose the title Fahrenheit 451 based on the physical temperature at which standard book paper ignites and burns.

questions.question: Which French-Algerian existentialist author wrote The Stranger and The Myth of Sisyphus, winning the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957?
questions.explanation: Camus developed the philosophy of the Absurd, illustrating human determination to find meaning in a silent universe.

questions.question: Which American author won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature for masterworks exploring African American history, including Beloved and Song of Solomon?
questions.explanation: Toni Morrison became the first Black woman of any nationality to win the Nobel Prize in Literature for her visionary language and historical depth.

questions.question: Which Irish playwright wrote the absurdist landmark Waiting for Godot, in which Vladimir and Estragon wait endlessly for an arrival?
questions.explanation: Beckett won the 1969 Nobel Prize in Literature for minimalist dramatic works that stripped away theatrical excess to expose human vulnerability.

questions.question: Which Indian polymath and poet wrote Gitanjali, becoming the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913?
questions.explanation: Tagore reshaped Bengali literature and music, composing the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.

questions.question: Which Japanese author was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1968 for poetic masterworks including Snow Country and Thousand Cranes?
questions.explanation: Kawabata was praised by the Nobel Committee for his narrative mastery, which with great sensibility expresses the essence of the Japanese mind.

questions.question: At what young age in years did Rudyard Kipling win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907, remaining the youngest literature laureate in history?
questions.explanation: Rudyard Kipling was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature at age 41 in 1907, a record for youth that remains unbroken over a century later.
